newsitem.title: USA: Apologetic Gingrich re-elected U.S. House Speaker.
newsitem.headline: Apologetic Gingrich re-elected U.S. House Speaker.

text.p: A contrite, apologetic Newt Gingrich was re-elected speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday in a close, dramatic vote that saw nine Republicans desert him because of ethics controversies.

Gingrich, under a cloud from ethics findings that may soon result in his being disciplined by the very House he leads, became the first Republican speaker to win re-election in successive Congresses in 68 years.
He accepted the honour with a conciliatory, forward-looking speech that included apologies to his colleagues and the country for any behaviour that caused offence or controversy.

"To the degree I was too brash, too self-confident or too pushy (during his first two-year term), I apologise," Gingrich, a Georgia conservative, said in his speech. "To whatever degree in any way that I have brought controversy or inappropriate attention to the House, I apologise."

The vote at the start of the 105th two-year Congress came one day before the House Ethics Committee was to begin the last phase of a two-year investigation that will conclude with a recommendation on punishment and a House vote on that.

Gingrich, architect of the Republican takeover of Congress two years ago, won re-election on Tuesday on a vote of 216-205. Five Republicans abstained and four backed others, believing he should not be re-elected under an ethics cloud.
Democrats voted for their leader, Richard Gephardt.

Republican leaders had consistently predicted Gingrich's re-election but worked hard to win over undecided colleagues. Gingrich appeared before party meetings on Monday night and Tuesday to answer questions and listen to members' concerns.
Democrats made a last-minute effort to delay the vote on the speakership but were blocked by Republicans, some of whom had also wanted a delay until the ethics issue was resolved.

Less that three hours after Gingrich took the speaker's gavel the ethics issue erupted again on the House floor and Republicans, in a virtual party line vote, denied a request for extra time for the concluding phase of the Gingrich investigation.
The ethics committee last month set a schedule calling for a House vote on penalties no later than Jan. 21 and proposed House rules set this as a cutoff date for the current ethics committee.
But the four-member bipartisan investigative subcommittee and its special counsel James Cole said earlier on Tuesday that to allow a fair and orderly process the vote would have to take place later.
Democrats sought to eliminate the Jan. 21 cutoff but the House voted 223-205 to stick with the date.
The partisan spat set the stage for continued controversy over the Gingrich affair certain to be fuelled by public hearings by the ethics committtee.

Gingrich has admitted he brought discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent the use of tax-exempt donations in what critics consider a partisan political activity -- a college course he taught -- and by misleading ethics committee investigators looking into the matter.
Democrats have kept up a drumbeat of attacks on him on ethics questions, while Republicans have tried to portray the issue as a political one rather than an ethical problem.
But Gingrich told the House that he hoped to work with every member.
Acknowledging he has been a lightning rod for controversy, he said, "it is my intention to do everything I can to work with every member of this Congress."
Gingrich left the House floor after the vote, accompanied by his mother and surrouned by television cameras. Asked how he felt, he said, "Good. I feel humble."
